title: ESPN's Dan Wetzel Suggests Michigan Could Have Used AI for $12 Million Investigation
excerpt: The provocative ESPN column questions whether Michigan needed to spend millions on a law firm probe whose conclusions, Wetzel argues, were already obvious to anyone paying attention.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Michigan's $12 million investigation yielded predictable conclusions, suggesting AI could have done it cheaper.
  • The probe involved nearly 300 interviews and over 20,000 documents, but only a 2,000-word summary was released.
  • Athletic director Warde Manuel will leave in 2026 after a decade of championships and scandals.
  • The article raises questions about AI's role in future institutional investigations and compliance oversight.

  • ESPN columnist Dan Wetzel argued Michigan's $12 million Jenner & Block investigation yielded conclusions so predictable that AI could have reached them at a fraction of the cost.
  • The probe interviewed nearly 300 people and reviewed over 20,000 documents, but Michigan released only a 2,000-word summary asserting attorney-client privilege.
  • Athletic director Warde Manuel will step down at end of 2026 after a decade marked by four national championships and a cascade of scandals.
  • The column raises broader questions about AI tools transforming institutional investigations and compliance oversight.

A $12 Million Question

When the University of Michigan announced on July 20 that athletic director Warde Manuel would step down following a seven-month investigation by Chicago law firm Jenner & Block, ESPN senior columnist Dan Wetzel offered a pointed take: the university could have run the whole investigation through artificial intelligence instead.

The column landed amid a flood of coverage about the $12 million probe. Jenner & Block interviewed nearly 300 witnesses, reviewed more than 20,000 documents, and fielded tips from over 90 people through a dedicated hotline. The result? A 2,000-word summary that found Manuel had demonstrated "important leadership strengths" but also identified "failures to quickly and effectively act on allegations of wrongdoing by Athletic Department employees."

Wetzel's argument was characteristically blunt: the conclusions were so widely anticipated that modern AI tools — capable of parsing documents, analyzing patterns, and synthesizing findings — could have produced similar results for a fraction of the cost.

> **"Former hockey coach Mel Pearson was let go amid misconduct allegations.

As USA Today's For The Win noted, Michigan's scandals have cost more than $37 million total."**

The Scandals That Made It Obvious

What made Wetzel's provocation resonate was the volume of publicly known failures that preceded the investigation. Under Manuel's decade-long watch, Michigan's athletic department accumulated an extraordinary list of controversies.

Former football coach Sherrone Moore was fired in December 2025 after executive assistant Paige Shiver revealed a years-long inappropriate relationship. Moore was arrested after entering Shiver's apartment, faced a felony charge, and ultimately pleaded no contest to lesser offenses. The Wall Street Journal reported Manuel had asked Moore to stop bringing Shiver on road trips before the 2024 season — suggesting awareness well before Moore's firing.

"This public university paid Jenner & Block $12 million to investigate the Sherrone Moore scandal and the abuse, yet now refuses to release the investigation's findings."

— Andrew M. Stroth, attorney for Paige Shiver

Before Moore, the Connor Stalions sign-stealing scandal overshadowed Michigan's 2023 national championship, resulting in roughly $30 million in NCAA fines. Former offensive coordinator Matt Weiss was indicted on federal charges for allegedly hacking student-athletes' accounts. Former basketball coach Juwan Howard was suspended for striking a Wisconsin assistant coach. Former hockey coach Mel Pearson was let go amid misconduct allegations.

As USA Today's For The Win noted, Michigan's scandals have cost more than $37 million total. Most fans could see Manuel's position was untenable — and it didn't cost them $12 million to reach that conclusion.

AI's Growing Role in Institutional Oversight

Scandals Under Manuel's Watch
›Sherrone Moore fired for inappropriate relationship.
›Connor Stalions sign-stealing scandal led to $30 million in fines.
›Matt Weiss indicted for hacking student-athletes' accounts.
›Juwan Howard suspended for striking an assistant coach.
›Total cost of Michigan's scandals exceeds $37 million.

Wetzel's column tapped into a rapidly accelerating conversation about AI in legal and investigative work. AI-powered document review tools have already transformed parts of the legal industry, with firms using them to flag compliance risks and synthesize findings from massive document sets at speeds human review cannot match.

The notion that AI could process 20,000-plus documents more efficiently than a team of lawyers is not far-fetched. E-discovery platforms powered by machine learning have been standard in large-scale litigation for years. Whether AI could handle the broader cultural assessment is more complex, but the column struck a nerve because the investigation's conclusions felt anticlimactic relative to the investment.

"The culture assessment is sobering. As a great university, we simply must do better."

— Domenico Grasso, University of Michigan Interim President

What Comes Next

Manuel will remain through the end of 2026 as a "special advisor" before departing. Grasso has launched a national search for a new athletic director — Michigan's third change in football coach, basketball coach, and AD within 13 months.

Michigan outlined reforms including a potential chief compliance officer, strengthened reporting systems, and an athletics advisory board. But the university declined to release the full Jenner & Block report, citing attorney-client privilege and pending litigation, including Shiver's Freedom of Information Act lawsuit.

Whether AI could truly replicate a complex institutional investigation is debatable. But Wetzel's column captured a growing sentiment: in an era when AI can process documents and generate analysis in minutes, spending $12 million on a law firm to produce conclusions that surprised no one feels like a relic of a pre-AI world.
